cells.tense: Right now you're charging forward and the line you set is one you also cross.
cells.act: ask the question you do not know the answer to
cells.ask: Take a conviction you carry and put a real question to somebody who'd know, one where the reply isn't already in your pocket.
cells.core:
You move first. You set a boundary by crossing it, and the momentum itself gives the cue — nobody has to be told where the front is. That's not noise. Things that sat still move when you're here, and the movement holds because you genuinely don't need permission to start.

The clearing keeps it honest. Something's been set down, so the charge isn't running on old fuel. What's left is to keep the motion from hardening into certainty. Ask a real question about the thing you're most sure of, to somebody who'd know, and hear the answer out before you argue with it. You'll still go first. You'll just be going toward something you checked.
cells.sheetLine: You already move first. Ask one question before you go.
cells.verb: charging forward first and setting the line by crossing it
cells.place: a clearing where what's finished gets set down

cells.tense: Tomorrow's version of this has already been decided, and today is just the runway.
cells.ask: Write the next three moves for something you're pushing, do the first, and wait until that one's done before touching the second.
cells.core:
You're ahead of where you are. Next month is already solid in your head, so what's happening now reads as the slow part before the real thing starts, and the people in it can feel themselves being moved toward a conclusion you've reached. The charge is real. It's just arriving somewhere nobody has agreed to yet.

The clearing gives you somewhere to put that. Three moves, written down, is enough to hold the shape without holding the whole month. Do the first, then wait until it's finished. The strategising stays yours; it stops being the place you live. Tomorrow stays unwritten a little longer, and the thing you're building gets built in an order it can actually be built in.

cells.tense: You were the one who moved first, and that door is behind you now.
cells.act: force the change into reality by steady effort
cells.ask: Give twenty minutes of steady effort to the change you keep circling: a call made, a form sent, a first piece finished.
cells.core:
The charge isn't running. You've been standing near the same decision, and from outside it looks like patience — you'd probably call it waiting for the right moment. The clearing already happened; something got released. But nothing new has been started in its place, and the space is just space.

So don't wait to feel decisive. Put twenty minutes of plain effort into the change you keep walking around: a call made, a form sent, a first piece finished — small enough that it doesn't need the feeling to arrive first. The charge comes back through the door of the work, not before it. Do that inch, and let the one after it wait its turn.

cells.tense: You're already steering this, and the story you tell has someone else at the wheel.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what serves
cells.ask: Look at what you're still carrying, name the part that's genuinely finished, set that part aside, and hold on to the rest.
cells.core:
Something here has your hand on it. When the group changes direction, you're usually the reason — a call made early, a line drawn before anyone noticed it needed drawing. Ask and you'd say it just went that way. The charge is doing its work through you, and the way you describe it leaves you out of the picture.

The clearing helps here. Look at what you're still carrying — a project, a role, a version of a plan — and name the part of it that's finished. Not the whole thing; the part that's done. Set that part aside and hold the rest. Deciding what stays and what goes is the charge in its plainest form, and doing it on paper means you see your own hand in it.

attempts.check: What I can't support: that the release in this seat has actually happened or that people are tired under the charge. All the record gives is the seat itself and the capacity; it doesn't say what has been let go or what a week would reveal. Reader's likely objection: 'I'm not gripping anything, I just move fast.' The ask survives that because choosing one thing to do on the person's behalf is still useful even if the read is wrong — it produces a visible result without requiring the person to first agree with the diagnosis. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is the one that makes the letting-go sound like a verdict on what they've been doing, so each cell names the capacity, not the person.
